title: Fourteen edits, six points, no suspect
spec: M30 · context as code — drift, attribution, regression gates
intro: A quarter of small prompt edits took UCC risk accuracy from 94% to 88%, and nobody can name the one that did it. The same quarter, replayed with versions, changelogs and a gate, turns the mystery into a line number and a rollback.

provenance.source: a narrated quarter of prompt changes on a UCC risk pipeline; version numbers, accuracy figures, and changelog entries are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: The discipline is M30's: version every context change with a changelog, gate it on the eval set before merge, stamp the version into your logs so drift is attributable, and keep every version rollback-able.

steps.title: The slow leak
narrative: In May the UCC risk pipeline scored 94% on the nightly eval set. In August it scores 88%. Nothing broke; there was never a bad day, only a slightly worse month than the one before it.

The system prompt lives in config/prompts.yaml. It has been edited about fourteen times this quarter — an example added, a sentence about tone, a retrieval k nudged, a compression budget trimmed, a guardrail phrase softened. Each was small, none was tested, and the file has one commit: "prompt tweaks", amended repeatedly.

So there is nothing to bisect. You cannot name which edit cost you six points, you cannot roll back to a good state because you cannot say which state was good, and the logs record answers against a prompt they never identified. This is context drift: not one bad change, a quarter of unmeasured ones.
steps.youDo: Run git log on the file that holds your system prompt. If it is under ten commits for a quarter of edits, your prompt is not under version control — it is under a filename.

terminal.text: which change dropped UCC risk accuracy from 94% to 88%?
git log --oneline -- config/prompts.yaml
b2c9f11  prompt tweaks   (amended 14 times, 2026-05-02 → 2026-08-19)
logs.group_by("prompt_version")
KeyError: 'prompt_version' — the field was never written
no per-version eval history · no changelog · no rollback target

view.text: Bisect (no versions), attribute (no stamps in the logs), roll back (no known-good target), or reproduce a June answer (the prompt that produced it no longer exists anywhere). The eval number is the only honest artifact you have, and it only tells you that something is wrong.

steps.title: Register the change instead of saving the file
narrative: Replay the same quarter with one rule: a context change is a registered version, not a file save. register() takes the prompt body, the retrieval and compression settings that travel with it, a changelog line saying what and why, and the eval result at the time of registration.
That last field is what makes the history useful. A changelog that says "trimmed the examples" is a diary; a changelog that says "trimmed the examples — 94.2% → 91.2%" is evidence.

And the version id is stamped into every observability record (M28), so from here on a log row knows which prompt produced it. Attribution is not a report you generate later; it is a field you write at call time or it does not exist.
steps.claudeSays: Same prompt text as before. The difference is that the string now has an id, a parent, a reason, and a number attached to it.
steps.youDo: Add prompt_version to your log payload today, even before you have a registry. Everything else in this walkthrough is impossible without that one field.

terminal.text:
registry.register(
    version="v31", parent="v30",
    prompt=open("prompts/ucc_risk.md").read(),
    settings={"retrieval_k": 5, "compress_budget": 4000},
    changelog="trim few-shot block — the 'termination filed but not posted' example looked redundant",
)
v31 registered · sha 4e1a77c · parent v30 · eval pending
observe.stamp("prompt_version")
every log record now carries prompt_version

lines: You are a UCC lien analyst. Grade debtor risk as LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH.
A termination is filed against 2024-FL-0019988 but has not posted.
The lien is still active. Grade HIGH and cite the filing id.
A debtor with no active filings grades LOW.

rows: trim few-shot block — the 'termination filed but not posted' example looked redundant

steps.title: The history answers in one query
narrative: With sixteen versions registered and stamped, the question that had no answer becomes a table sorted by version. The six points are not spread evenly across fourteen edits — two edits own five and a half of them and the other twelve are noise.

v31 removed the edge case that taught the model what a filed-but-unposted termination means. Accuracy fell 94.2% to 91.2% and the misses concentrate exactly there: on the 34 borderline filings, not across the board. v37 cut the compression budget from 4,000 tokens to 2,500 to save money, and cost the filing identifiers the answers have to cite — 90.8% to 88.3%.

That is the whole payoff of versioning. Not that it prevents a bad change, but that it makes a bad change nameable — a version, a date, an author, a changelog line, and the stratum where the damage landed. "The slide started at v31 on May 14" is a thing you can act on. "Accuracy is down this quarter" is not.
steps.youDo: Plot eval accuracy against version id rather than against calendar time. Steps in that chart are changes; slopes are noise.

terminal.text: eval accuracy by prompt version, v25 through v40
registry.history(metric="eval_accuracy", detect="step_change")
step change at v31: -3.0pp  (r.mensah, 2026-05-14, "trim few-shot block")
step change at v37: -2.5pp  (d.alvarez, 2026-07-08, "compress_budget 4000 → 2500 to cut cost")
residual across the other 12 versions: -0.5pp — within noise

view.text: 94% in May, 88% in August, fourteen undated edits and no way to tell a real regression from ordinary variation. Every proposed fix — rewrite it, freeze it, add more examples — is itself an untested change.

after.title: AFTER — two versions own the slide

steps.title: The gate, and the way back
narrative: Attribution explains the past; the gate stops the next one. Every registered candidate runs the M29 eval set before it can merge, and a drop in accuracy, a rise in cost, or a fall in the safety pass rate blocks it. Candidate v41 adds "be concise" to the system prompt, scores 85.2% against the v40 baseline of 88.0%, and never reaches production. It also rewrites the cached prefix, so the gate reports the cache and memory it would have invalidated — a prompt change is a migration, not an edit.

Then walk back the two you now have names for. Restore the v31 example and lift the compression budget to 4,000, registered as v42 with the changelog saying which regressions it reverses. It scores 93.5% — the 0.7 points that do not come back are the honest cost of a quarter spent without a gate.

Roll out with the discipline the mechanism assumes: pin the version per request, canary 10% of traffic, keep v40 live and rollback-able, and let the old cached prefixes expire rather than serving two prompts under one cache key.
steps.claudeSays: v41 was blocked by a number, not by an opinion. That is the only kind of block that survives a disagreement.
steps.youDo: Wire your eval set into CI as a required check on the prompt directory. A gate that runs after merge is a report; a gate that runs before it is a gate.

terminal.text: gate(candidate="v41", baseline="v40", eval_set="ucc-200")
v41  accuracy 85.2%  (baseline 88.0%)   cost $0.0199  safety 40/40
⛔ MERGE BLOCKED — accuracy -2.8pp vs baseline · would invalidate a 7,100-token cached prefix and 1,204 memory keys bound to v40

registry.register(version="v42", parent="v40",
    changelog="restore the v31 termination example; compress_budget 2500 → 4000 (reverts v37)")
gate(candidate="v42", baseline="v40", eval_set="ucc-200")
v42  accuracy 93.5%  (+5.5pp)   cost $0.0207   safety 40/40   — MERGE ALLOWED
canary 10% · v40 held for rollback · rollback("v40") verified in 1 call

view.note: the end of a quarter of untracked edits — no single culprit, and no way back

views.text: The prompt is code now: every change has an id, a parent, a reason and a number; a regression is blocked before it ships; a log row names the version that produced it; and rollback is one call. Drift does not stop happening — it stops being invisible, which is the only part you can engineer.
